content:
Philip Ruddock, a former Liberal minister, has been appointed by cabinet to review whether Australian law adequately protects religious freedom as a human right. This appointment comes in the context of the same-sex marriage debate and is intended to prevent a contentious dispute over religious amendments in upcoming marriage equality legislation.

***

The timing and approach to religious freedom protections has divided senior government members. While Treasurer Scott Morrison maintains that the review is "no substitute" for religious amendments in the marriage bill itself, other conservatives like Peter Dutton and Mathias Cormann support addressing religious freedom through separate legislation next year. Morrison and Senator David Fawcett, however, insist these issues must be considered simultaneously with the marriage bill.

***

Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull has emphasized the need for careful consideration of religious freedom issues following the yes vote on marriage equality. He noted that while various proposals for legislative changes have emerged in recent months, many extend beyond the immediate marriage question and require careful scrutiny by parliament.

***

Turnbull warned about the risks associated with hasty legislation on fundamental rights, expressing particular concern about "generally worded bill of rights-style declarations" that could create legal uncertainties. He stressed that any reforms protecting religious freedom must be undertaken carefully to avoid unintended consequences.

***

The review, which Ruddock must complete by March 31, is described as a "timely expert stocktake" to guide any necessary legislative reforms. Turnbull endorsed Ruddock as the appropriate person for this task, citing his previous experience as Australia's special envoy for human rights.
